facts.claim: Del Water Gap's 'Quilt of Steam' is a collaboration with Arlo Parks. It is a single from his album 'I Miss You Already + I Haven't Left Yet', which was set for release on 29 September 2023 via Mom + Pop.
Songwriting credits for 'Quilt of Steam' go to Samuel Holden Jaffe, Anais Marinho (Arlo Parks) and Ethan Gruska.
Production credits go to Samuel Holden Jaffe and Ethan Gruska. Michael Freeman mixed the song and Joe LaPorta mastered it.
Performer credits list Jaffe on vocals, Arlo Parks on vocals and Ethan Gruska on background vocals.

Jaffe says he and Arlo Parks toured together on her first album and became friends over a shared love of poetry and instrumental music. Both were burned out. When they got time off they spent two days with Ethan Gruska, and 'Quilt of Steam' is the phrase that stuck.

Jaffe says the song is about coming off tour feeling scrambled and looking for balance and stillness. It describes waking in his own bed after months away and watching steam rise off the radiator. He also calls it a song about finding beauty in the mundane and about the 'treason' of not acknowledging conflict.

W Magazine describes the song, written with and featuring Arlo Parks, as one that processes returning from tour. It sits on a 12-song album whose title comes from a grandfather's inscription to his grandmother in a book of William Carlos Williams poetry.
Del Water Gap is the solo project of Brooklyn-based songwriter and producer S. Holden Jaffe. He was born in New Haven, CT, and attended NYU's Clive Davis Institute of Recorded Music.
Earlier in his catalog, Jaffe had the streaming hit 'High Tops' (2017). His major-label debut, 'Don't Get Dark', came in 2019, and a self-titled second LP followed in 2021.

Jaffe says he took the name Del Water Gap from a Sharpie scrawl on the back of a box truck. He wrote it on a list of band names while in a noise-rock band in high school, and later learned it was a national park.

research.lineage: It sits in the intimate, poetry-minded bedroom-pop and indie folk-pop tradition of Brooklyn songwriter-producers, and it is built on an indie collaboration with Arlo Parks.

draft:
The steam comes first. **Quilt of Steam** opens on someone coming to in their own bedroom after a month of not knowing where they were, finally noticing the heat lifting off the radiator. Del Water Gap's S. Holden Jaffe has said that's the literal scene: waking in his own bed after months on tour, scrambled, hunting for some stillness. The line "saw the quilt of steam rise off the radiator" turns a clanking apartment fixture into bedding, something soft and handmade. Then the verse makes the quilt the narrator's own work, layers stitched by hand that they're now sweating through, stretching on for acres. Comfort and smothering live in the same image.

The phrase came out of two days Jaffe spent with Arlo Parks and producer Ethan Gruska. Jaffe and Parks had toured together on her first album and bonded over poetry and instrumental music, and both were burned out. All three share the writing credit, and Parks and Gruska both sing on the track. That image-first instinct puts the song with the poetry-minded bedroom-pop and indie folk-pop of Brooklyn songwriter-producers. Fittingly, the album it leads into takes its title from a grandfather's inscription in a book of William Carlos Williams poems.

What makes it hurt is how honest the narrator is about their own silence. The verses ask for so little: that the other person stop for a second and sit, that they bring up the thing while the narrator waits in the car. But the narrator never brings it up either. They keep "folding clothes alone as if it wasn't treason," and Jaffe has named that treason plainly as not acknowledging conflict. Resentment and self-indictment sit side by side. The narrator plays the stoic captain with no compass and begs to be held until it passes, and the song never decides which one is true. The chorus admits what the scene couldn't: "I couldn't admit I was crushed by the weight of being strangers." The confession only happens inside the song.

The sound refuses to mope. Drums drive a four-on-the-floor beat with a prominent snare, the bass holds to root notes, acoustic guitar strums under a clean electric, and a synth pad warms the back of the mix. It's polished, each part in its own space, with reverb opening up the vocal and drums. The lead voice is clear and direct, a little urgent, as if the words have to get out before the nerve goes. And the lyric closes by running that crushed chorus twice more, saying it until it finally lands.

It puts you in that parked car, each person waiting for the other to speak, and makes you feel how lonely that kind of politeness gets.
